clue.text: Realistic show must be awful crap to amuse (they say) the awful cast

indicators.note: something awful is in a dreadful state, so the word after it is jumbled into a new order
what people say is heard rather than read, so the phrase before it is wanted only for its sound

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
to tickle someone is to amuse them; the ending of a word like 'tactical' is said the same way
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A critic sneers that a supposedly realistic production is rubbish, with a dreadful cast.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is in two lights, 1 and 6 across. Both pieces read as words: a realistic show is a practical one, and Cats is the show; T.S. Eliot's Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats inspired the musical.
explanation.definitionFit: Realistic means practical, and Cats is the famous stage musical, so a sensible musical is wittily read as these words.

clue.text: With loads of room for the "i" in "semivowel"

indicators.note: putting the letter in the word means it is placed inside that word

blocks.note: a palatal is a sound made with the tongue against the hard palate, such as the semivowel y
the letter itself

explanation.surface: A phonetics note about where the letter i sits in the word semivowel.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks suggest we look at the letters of 'semivowel' itself, but it must be replaced by a kind of semivowel before the i goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: A palatial building is grand like a palace, so it has space in abundance.

clue.text: Essential for lamb learning to walk

indicators.note: what is essential to something lies at its core, so the letters sit inside the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A newborn lamb needs something before it can take its first steps.
explanation.definitionFit: To amble is to stroll at an easy, leisurely pace on foot.

clue.text: Slides that can't be hidden?

blocks.note: surface reading: photographic slides or sheets for an overhead projector
setter's reading: things so clear that you can see right through them, so nothing about them is concealed

explanation.walkthrough: Projector slides are called by a name that also describes anything see-through, which is why they cannot hide anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Overhead projector sheets and photographic slides are named for being see-through, and anything see-through conceals nothing.

clue.text: Many outside Tyneside should be hit on the head

indicators.note: one thing outside another wraps round it, holding it within

blocks.note: a crowd is many people
Tyneside, around Newcastle, is in England's North East, abbreviated NE

explanation.surface: A mob in the North East is getting violent and someone is going to be clobbered.
explanation.definitionFit: To crown someone is informal slang for striking them on the top of the skull.

clue.text: Having had some lager - dead drunk at the start - his problem?

definitions.text: Having had some lager - dead drunk at the start - his problem?

indicators.note: only some of the word is wanted, here its opening part
the words just before are wanted only for their opening letters
a problem is something to be worked out, so the letters of the word next to it must be sorted

blocks.note: the first two letters of this word
the first letter of each word
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A young man has had a few beers and was legless early on; is drink his problem?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition as well as the wordplay: the lad who drinks lager until he is drunk is behaving in this way.
explanation.definitionFit: Laddish behaviour is the loud, boozy conduct of young men out drinking beer together.

clue.text: See 1
Sailor drunk retsina, which I wouldn't do

indicators.note: drunk means unsteady and muddled, so the word after it is jumbled

blocks.note: an able-bodied seaman is an AB
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A seaman has knocked back the Greek wine, which the teetotal speaker would never do.
explanation.walkthrough: The speaker of the clue, who would not drink retsina, is the answer, so the definition works in the first person.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who abstains refuses alcohol, so the speaker who would never drink wine is one.

clue.text: Crime is up when you get cash without energy

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the word is read from bottom to top
cash without a letter means the cash has that letter taken away

blocks.note: taken as written
cash is money
E is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: Crime rises whenever people can get money without effort.
explanation.definitionFit: Simony is the ecclesiastical offence of buying or selling church posts or pardons.

clue.text: With scorn I leave police: you mustn't worry

indicators.note: if I leave, that letter departs from the word next to it
to worry something is to shake and tug it about, so these letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written, before the letter departs
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone sneers as they resign from the force, telling a colleague not to fret.
explanation.definitionFit: To act contemptuously is to behave with open disdain and derision toward others.

clue.text: Sign of opposition to Tory big guns?

blocks.note: the Liberals were the traditional rival party of the Conservatives in Britain
the Royal Artillery, the army's gunners

explanation.surface: Is there an emblem showing resistance to the Conservative heavyweights?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big guns' looks like party grandees but means the Royal Artillery.
explanation.definitionFit: Libra, the scales, is one of the twelve signs of the zodiac.

clue.text: Senior citizens' concession returned, all with book of 1 6

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: the old are the senior citizens
a sop is a small concession made to pacify someone
the sum is the whole, all of it

explanation.surface: A pensioners' discount has been brought back, along with a volume of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 6 is the answer to 1 and 6 across, and the book is T.S. Eliot's Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats; Old Possum was Ezra Pound's nickname for Eliot.
explanation.definitionFit: The cat poems are titled as belonging to this persona, so the owner of that book is him.

clue.text: Crime needs time and cause

blocks.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time
a cause is a reason

explanation.surface: Committing an offence requires opportunity and motive.
explanation.definitionFit: Treason, betraying one's country or sovereign, is the gravest criminal offence against the state.

clue.text: Progressing along lines?

blocks.note: first meaning: under way and advancing, as a plan is
second meaning, read literally: aboard a carriage running on railway lines

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for under way is also, read literally, where a rail passenger is.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means arranged and under way, and a rail passenger travelling the tracks is literally aboard a carriage.

clue.text: Opening of epic play - what can hold a note in song, if historic

blocks.note: first meaning: the start of Virgil's Aeneid, 'Arma virumque cano', in Dryden's English
second meaning: George Bernard Shaw's 1894 comedy

blocks.clueFragment: what can hold a note in song, if historic
blocks.note: a playful gloss: arms can hold a note, and the epic line goes on 'I sing', a song of history

explanation.walkthrough: Shaw took his title from the Aeneid's opening, 'Arms and the man I sing'; the last part of the clue is a further hint, since limbs hold things and an epic is history sung.
explanation.definitionFit: Virgil's Aeneid begins with these words in English translation, and Shaw borrowed them to title his comedy.

clue.text: Mother's sovereign keeping one from Channel Island is partisan

indicators.note: keeping something means holding it inside, so one word goes within the other
one letter is taken from the island's name, leaving it short

blocks.note: Ma is mother; the 's means 'has'
a sovereign is a pound coin, informally a quid
Sark is one of the Channel Islands

explanation.surface: Mum's gold coin holds something from the Channel Islands, revealing her as a resistance fighter.
explanation.walkthrough: The island loses its last letter before going inside the coin, between its I and D. A sovereign is an old British gold pound coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A maquisard was a member of the French wartime Resistance, a guerrilla partisan fighter.

clue.text: Absentee of 1 6 makes a hole under mountain

indicators.note: in a down entry, under means placed lower down, so the second part comes after the first

blocks.note: M is the map abbreviation for mountain
a cavity is a hole

explanation.surface: Someone missing digs a pit at the foot of a peak.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'under' places the hole below the mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: In Eliot's cat poems the Mystery Cat is famous for never being there when a crime is discovered.

clue.text: Antique cover - one managed to survive into last century

definitions.text: one managed to survive into last century

blocks.note: first meaning: the monarch whose head appears on the stamps of an old philatelic envelope, called a cover

blocks.clueFragment: one managed to survive into last century
blocks.note: second meaning: the monarch who died in January 1901, just inside the twentieth century

explanation.walkthrough: To stamp collectors a cover is a posted envelope; an old one bears the Penny Black with this monarch's head.
explanation.definitionFit: The long-reigning Victorian monarch appears on early postage stamps and died in 1901, after the twentieth century began.

clue.text: No fishing possible with such a financial result?

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: when a fisherman's mesh has gone missing he cannot fish
second meaning: the bottom line in accounts when costs exceed income

explanation.walkthrough: The accounting term is read literally as the disappearance of a fishing mesh.
explanation.definitionFit: In accounts, the overall deficit after expenses exceed income is the figure described here, and a missing mesh stops any angling.

clue.text: I don't believe in God's last entry into new life

indicators.note: only the final letter of the word before is wanted
a new version is a remade one, so the word after it is rearranged
an entry into something goes inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, to be rearranged
the last letter of God

explanation.surface: An atheist speaks: God's final arrival into a new existence is not credible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I don't believe in God' reads as one statement, but 'in' is the start of the wordplay; the definition is in the first person, the speaker being the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An infidel is a person without religious faith, an unbeliever, as the speaker declares.

clue.text: House the French talk about

indicators.note: about means round the outside, so one word wraps the other

blocks.note: to talk is to chat
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A home that people in France gossip about.
explanation.definitionFit: A chalet is a wooden Swiss-style dwelling, often a holiday cabin.

clue.text: Cover sheltering most of circus was fatal to Samson

definitions.note: a description of the answer, not a synonym

indicators.note: to shelter something is to keep it under cover, enclosed
only most of the word is wanted, so some letters are shed from it

blocks.note: a hat is a head covering
taken as written, before trimming both ends

explanation.surface: A canopy over the big top proved the death of the strongman from the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: Here 'most of' removes both the first and last letters. Samson lost his strength when Delilah had his hair cut, which led to his death.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible, having his locks shorn stripped Samson of strength and led to his downfall.

clue.text: State backing for Irish imprisoned by Hitler

indicators.note: someone imprisoned by another is held within them
backing means going in reverse, so the result is read from the end

blocks.note: Hitler's first name
IR is the abbreviation for Irish

explanation.surface: A nation supporting an Irishman locked up by the Nazi dictator.
explanation.definitionFit: Florida is one of the fifty states of the USA, in the far south-east.

clue.text: I don't do much that is of not so much use

blocks.note: first meaning: a lazy person, speaking of themselves
second meaning: comparative of an adjective for something unused or pointless

explanation.surface: Someone admits to laziness and to being rather less useful than before.
explanation.definitionFit: A lazybones is one who does little, and the comparative of idle means more inactive or more futile.

clue.text: Tenure terminable by bullets blasting holes in it?

indicators.note: blasting something blows it apart, so the letters of the word after it are scattered
the result goes inside the bullets, which 'it' refers back to

blocks.note: bullets are made of lead, and the metal stands for them
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A property right that can be ended by gunfire tearing through it.
explanation.definitionFit: Leasehold is holding property for a fixed term under a lease, which eventually expires.

clue.text: Dominant, the leading note of the conductor?

blocks.note: in sol-fa the fifth degree of the scale, the dominant, is sol
the seventh degree, the leading note, is ti in sol-fa

explanation.surface: Asks whether a dominating maestro sets the first note for his orchestra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dominant' and 'leading' sound like personality traits of a maestro, but both are technical names for degrees of the scale.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Georg Solti was a celebrated Hungarian-British conductor, long at Covent Garden and Chicago.

clue.text: In and out of season?

blocks.note: first meaning: the sea's flow that comes in and goes out twice a day
second meaning: an old word for a time of year, as in Christmastide

explanation.walkthrough: 'In and out of season' sounds like a fruit's availability; it is two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea's rise and fall comes in and goes out, and archaic usage gives a festival time like Eastertide.

clue.text: Girl playing Mary in religious body

indicators.note: someone playing a part takes on a new form, so the name after it is rearranged

blocks.note: Sally is a girl's name
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A girl takes the role of the Virgin Mary in a church group's nativity play.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sally Army is a British nickname for the Salvation Army.
explanation.definitionFit: The Salvation Army is a Christian church and charity organised on military lines.
